Pro Cycling Manager 2024 offers an incredibly detailed and immersive experience for cycling enthusiasts and sports management fans alike, continuing the series’ tradition of blending realism with deep strategic gameplay. Developed by Cyanide Studio, this iteration refines many aspects of team management, race tactics, and rider development while introducing subtle improvements that enhance the overall simulation without alienating newcomers. Players step into the shoes of a professional cycling team manager, responsible for recruiting riders, planning training schedules, managing budgets, and devising race strategies across an extensive calendar of events including grand tours, one-day classics, and smaller circuit races. The game’s depth lies in its intricate systems that simulate the physical and psychological conditions of riders, the impact of terrain and weather, and the ever-shifting dynamics of pelotons, all of which demand careful planning and real-time decision-making during races.

One of the standout features of Pro Cycling Manager 2024 is its expanded race-day tactics interface, which offers more granular control over rider roles, pacing, and breakaways. This allows players to execute complex strategies like setting tempo on climbs, organizing lead-outs for sprints, or conserving energy for critical moments with precision. The AI behavior has been improved to present a more realistic peloton, reacting dynamically to attacks and environmental factors, making races unpredictable and thrilling. Additionally, the game’s new scouting and development system encourages long-term planning, as nurturing young talent becomes as crucial as managing star riders. Training modules are deeper, with an emphasis on balancing intensity and recovery, directly influencing performance and injury risk.

Graphically, the game continues to impress with detailed rider models, realistic race environments, and smooth animations that bring the excitement of professional cycling to life. The broadcast-style camera work and race commentary add to the immersion, making race simulations feel authentic and engaging. Off the bike, the management menus are comprehensive but accessible, offering plenty of statistics and data visualization tools to inform tactical decisions without overwhelming players. The inclusion of historical teams and riders, as well as updated rosters for the 2024 season, enhances the game’s appeal to fans who appreciate accuracy and nostalgia.

While Pro Cycling Manager 2024 excels in depth and realism, it may present a steep learning curve for newcomers unfamiliar with the nuances of professional cycling or management sims. Some users might find the interface dense, and the slower pace compared to traditional sports games requires patience and strategic thinking. Additionally, while the single-player experience is robust, the multiplayer modes could benefit from further polish and matchmaking improvements to fully capitalize on competitive play. Minor technical issues and occasional AI quirks also emerge but rarely detract from the overall enjoyment.

In summary, Pro Cycling Manager 2024 is a triumph for fans of cycling and sports management, offering an unparalleled level of detail and strategic complexity that rewards dedication and thoughtful planning. Its realistic simulation of the sport’s physical, tactical, and managerial aspects makes it a must-have for anyone seeking to experience the thrills and challenges of leading a professional cycling team to victory. Whether navigating the grueling climbs of the Tour de France or orchestrating a perfect sprint finish, this title captures the spirit and excitement of professional cycling with impressive authenticity and depth.

If one were to take the most engaging elements of Pro Cycling Manager and Tour de France, we’d have a cycling game that could finally do justice to both the tactical and visceral sides of the sport. Unfortunately, what we have are two games that, frankly, feel like half-hearted attempts at giving fans a complete experience, forcing players to settle for a disjointed rendition of what should be one immersive cycling journey.

With Pro Cycling Manager, you get the deep, spreadsheet-like tactics that emphasise the back-end management and strategic decision-making required to build and sustain a successful cycling team. You manage everything from training schedules to sponsorship and race-day tactics, focusing on long-term success. However, the graphics, user interface, and actual game-play mechanics feel trapped in the past. It’s a strategy game bogged down by outdated visuals and a clunky interface that has seen minimal evolution over the years. The tactical depth is there, but the game's execution feels stuck, with minimal updates between iterations and little done to address player feedback.

On the other hand, Tour de France captures the on-road experience better, allowing players to feel the adrenaline of navigating tight pelotons, managing breakaways, and dealing with the high-stakes moments of the sport. Yet, it suffers from its own setbacks: the graphics, while a slight improvement, still feel below par for modern sports games, and the gameplay mechanics feel more repetitive than rewarding. There’s excitement to be had in controlling a cyclist, but the repetitiveness of button-mashing and the lack of immersive tactics make it feel more like a racing game reskinned for cycling than an authentic simulation. It tries to capture the thrill of racing but loses the broader scope and strategy that define the Tour.

The worst part of this is that Pro Cycling Manager and Tour de France essentially ask players to pay twice for what should be a single, cohesive experience. By splitting up the strategic depth and in-race action across two games, it almost seems as though the developers are intentionally segmenting the experience to milk cycling fans for all they’re worth. Rather than building a robust, all-encompassing title that gives players both the thrill of racing and the satisfaction of strategic team management, the studio has chosen to slice the core of the sport in half, delivering two outdated, incomplete products that fail to elevate the genre or respect the fanbase.

Imagine a game that lets you both manage and race—a game where your meticulously prepared training plans and tactical decisions are put to the test as you control your riders in real-time. A game where you can plan a breakaway and then jump in to experience the tension and exhilaration of leading it. Instead, we’re stuck in a repetitive cycle (pun intended) of half-experiences that only further highlight how much potential is going to waste. With the technology and innovation available today, there’s no reason to settle for these compromises.

What we really should have is Tour de France as the cyclist career mode within Pro Cycling Manager. Instead of locking players into a season that doesn’t include the Giro d’Italia, Vuelta a España, or any real progression, an integrated career mode would give us the experience of a full pro cycling career. In this combined game, Tour de France wouldn’t just be a standalone racing game but would serve as the ultimate athlete career experience within Pro Cycling Manager. Players could start as rookies, working up through the ranks to face the world’s best cyclists in iconic races. They’d have the chance to participate in all the major tours and Spring Classics, with every season offering new goals and growth opportunities in a continuous career arc.

This integration would bring real synergy, allowing players to build a strategic, multi-year training schedule and then jump into specific races to test their skills. Each victory or defeat would feel meaningful, adding depth to the long-term career journey rather than isolated moments of achievement. Every decision, from training plans to contract negotiations, would impact the road ahead, making it a true simulation of a pro cyclist’s life where sacrifices, strategy, and hard work shape every season.

In summary, cycling fans deserve a single, unified game that combines both the depth of Pro Cycling Manager with the immediacy of Tour de France, delivering a title that is finally worthy of the sport’s complexity and excitement. Until the developers realise that, fans are left with two half-games that feel more like cash grabs than genuine passion projects. And in the end, cycling fans deserve better.

I've been a fan of the Pro Cycling Manager series for more than 10 years, but the latest 2024 edition hasn’t been great. The graphics still look outdated like they’re from 2010 and aren't even well optimized. The AI is also overly simplistic, almost like what you’d expect in a game for little kids. I was aware of these long-standing issues, so I decided to wait two weeks after release before buying the game, hoping for some improvements.

Sadly, the game remains almost unplayable with no significant new features added. It’s frustrating because these problems have been known and reported for a decade now. Considering the current state of the game, it looks like it will take at least another week before being able to play a game without gamebreaking bugs.

For those thinking about getting Pro Cycling Manager 2024, I’d say the game is worth no more than €20. Spending only this much will give you more value for your money and minimizes funding to the developers who have not addressed these persistent issues effectively.
